# Notes Written Before Anyone Procures a Tool

*Deliberately before. The moment "communication" becomes a workstream, it acquires a platform evaluation, a charter, and a set of norms everyone signs and nobody reads. We'll pick the suite with the nicest threading model, and threading was never the constraint.*

---

## The sentence I'd want taken apart

"Communication delays and occasional misunderstandings, impacting project timelines and team cohesion."

That sentence describes at least four unrelated conditions, and they take incompatible treatments. Nobody has said which one we have. I'd want a month and access to something more honest than a survey before letting anyone budget against it.

**Latency.** Genuine physics. Nine timezones, a question asked at 4pm in one place answered at 9am the next day in another, and a workflow with four handoffs in it — which is therefore a four-day workflow no matter how motivated anyone is. Treatment: re-cut the work. Nothing to do with how people talk.

**Coupling.** The delays are not delays in *communication*, they're delays in *permission*. Every rung of an approval ladder that crosses a timezone costs a day. Three rungs is three days, before anyone has thought about the actual problem. Treatment: move decision rights, not messages.

**Asymmetry.** There is a room somewhere — a floor, a corridor, a lunch table — where things get decided, and everyone else receives the decision as weather. What gets logged afterwards as a "misunderstanding" is very often the polite term for *we weren't in the room, and the version that reached us had already been smoothed*. Treatment: unpleasant and structural, and not available from a vendor.

**Register.** Real cross-cultural signal loss. Silence read as consent. "That's interesting" heard as interest. A team that cannot contradict a senior person on an open call, and therefore doesn't, and is therefore recorded as having agreed. Treatment: mechanisms that don't require anyone to change their personality.

My suspicion is that it's mostly the second and third, that the fourth is doing the work of making the first two look like a people problem, and that the first is what gets funded — because latency is the only one of the four that can be addressed without anyone senior giving anything up.

**So the first artefact isn't a communications plan. It's a wait-state log.** For four weeks, every person records each time they were blocked: blocked on what, on whom, in which timezone, for how long, and what eventually unblocked it. Alongside it, a corpus of actual misunderstandings — the real threads, verbatim, not a summary of themes. And a decision map: where decisions are *supposed* to be made against where they were *actually* made, which is a document that tends to embarrass people, which is why it's worth having.

Most organisations have never seen any of this, because the reporting runs on milestones, and a milestone tells you a thing was late without ever telling you which hour of the delay was real work and which was somebody asleep.

---

## The two things being conflated

**Communication and coordination.** They are not the same instrument. You can raise communication volume indefinitely — more standups, more channels, more all-hands — and *reduce* coordination, because every synchronous hour is a tax collected disproportionately from whoever is awake at an inconvenient time, and paid in the currency that coordination actually needs, which is uninterrupted thinking. A team that talks constantly and still ships late is not under-communicating. It is over-coupled.

**Cohesion and rapport.** Rapport is a virtual happy hour and a Slack channel for pets. Cohesion is behavioural and visible only under load: does someone in one region voluntarily pick up work for someone in another, without being asked, at a cost to themselves? Does anyone defend an absent colleague in a meeting they can't attend? That is the only cohesion worth measuring, and it isn't produced by socialising. It's produced by the discovery that the other side does what it says it will do.

Which points at the asymmetry I'd build on. Distributed teams suffer a systematic distortion: **absent context, delay reads as disrespect and brevity reads as contempt.** The same terse reply from someone at the next desk is read as busy; from someone on another continent it is read as a message. Every distributed team is quietly manufacturing grievances out of nothing but missing information about the other person's Tuesday. Fix the visibility of circumstance and a surprising volume of "conflict" evaporates before it needs resolving.

---

## Where I'd actually put the effort

**Make the written record the only record.** Not a documentation initiative — a rule with teeth: *a decision that isn't in the thread doesn't bind anyone.* If it was made in a corridor, it gets relitigated when the other continent wakes up. That is expensive enough, once or twice, that corridor decisions stop. The written default is the only mechanism I know that equalises across timezones without asking anyone to be awake, and it has a side effect worth more than the primary one: writing forces the reasoning into view, and most misunderstandings are disagreements about reasoning that were never surfaced because nobody had to state it.

**Cut the seams where the clock already cuts.** Conway's law, run backwards. Give each location something it can finish end-to-end without waking anyone. Count the handoffs in your critical workflows and multiply by twenty-four hours — that number is your real schedule, and no amount of goodwill moves it. Most "communication problems" in distributed teams are ownership problems wearing a costume. If two continents must confer daily to make progress, the work was cut wrongly, and the meeting is the symptom.

**Delete escalation rungs before adding anything.** Same argument as ever, but here the cost is denominated in days rather than in patience. Whoever is nearest the work decides, and tells everyone afterwards in writing. If we've assembled a team we can't trust to decide, the problem is upstream of the process, and no tool will reach it.

**Rotate the pain of the clock, and publish the ledger.** A standing meeting fixed at a time convenient to one city is a daily broadcast about whose sleep is discretionary. Rotate it, ruthlessly, including the ones senior people attend — *especially* those. Better: kill most of them. And keep a visible tally of meeting-hours falling outside working hours, by location. Not as a metric with a target. As a document that is simply true and that people can see.

**Then spend the surviving synchronous time on the only things it's good for.** Disagreement, ambiguity, and the first four weeks of a new relationship. Never status. Status is a document, and a status meeting is a document being read aloud to people who could have read it faster.

**Build channels where dissent is cheap.** This is the whole cross-cultural question, and the usual answer — train everyone to be more direct — is both futile and slightly insulting. Direct contradiction of a senior person in a public forum is simply unavailable to a large fraction of any global team, and it is not a deficit. So route around it. Written comments on a document before the call, so objections arrive without a face attached. Silent reading at the top of a meeting, then round-robin — everyone speaks, in turn, so that saying nothing requires an active choice. Objections gathered privately and carried into the room by whoever has the standing to voice them. And a hard norm, worth repeating until it's tedious: **silence is not agreement.** It is the single most expensive misreading available, and the cost lands three months later as rework.

**Treat English as the second language it is for most of the room.** The problem is almost never the non-native speakers. It's the native ones — pace, idiom, sports metaphors, humour that depends on being from somewhere, and the peculiar British and American habit of encoding refusal as mild enthusiasm. Anyone who speaks it as a first language should be asked, quietly, to slow down and say what they mean. And every verbally-agreed decision should be followed by a short written restatement from *the person who received it*, not the person who issued it — which surfaces the gap in the cheapest possible place.

**Make circumstance visible.** Calendars open, load visible, local holidays on everyone's view, an away signal that means something. Nearly free, and it starves the attribution error that manufactures most distributed conflict.

**Front-load the face-to-face, and mind the direction of travel.** A small amount of shared physical time early buys an enormous amount of interpretive charity later — people who have eaten together read each other's terse messages generously for about a year. Two observations though. Spend it at the start of a team's life, not as an annual reward. And send the centre to the periphery rather than the reverse: who flies to whom is read as a statement about who matters, and it is read correctly.

**One named human per interface.** Not a team alias, not a channel. A person who owns the seam between two workstreams and does not hand off. Continuity of ownership is what people mean when they say a project "felt well run."

**Point the machine at the seam.** Automatic transcription and summary of every synchronous session, searchable, so that being asleep is no longer the same as being absent. Translation where it helps. Anything that turns synchronous events into asynchronous artefacts. The test: does the technology reduce the number of people who need to be awake simultaneously, or does it just add another place to be interrupted?

---

## When it's already a conflict

Two distinctions worth holding.

**Task conflict is an asset and relationship conflict is a liability**, and distributed work converts the first into the second faster than co-located work does, because there's no corridor afterwards in which to repair it. So the intervention is timing, not content: intervene early and lightly rather than late and formally.

**Medium discipline.** The worst possible venue for a live disagreement is slow written ping-pong across a twelve-hour gap — each party spends half a day interpreting the last message in the least generous available way, and drafts accordingly. A simple rule earns its keep: *two round-trips of disagreement in text, then a call, whatever the hour.* And whoever proposes the call takes the inconvenient end of it.

**Who arbitrates.** Not the most senior person, and definitely not the most senior person from one of the two sites involved. Someone with relevant expertise and no stake in the outcome, chosen for credibility rather than rank. Arbitration by hierarchy in a cross-border dispute doesn't resolve anything; it just tells the losing side that the geography decided, and they'll remember.

---

## Measurement, which is where this normally dies

I'd retire response time, meeting attendance, and every tool-engagement statistic on sight. They measure compliance with the ritual, and they reward the behaviour we're trying to reduce.

What I'd watch instead: **blocked hours per person-week, by cause** — the honest version of "delays," and the only one that distinguishes physics from permission; **decision latency**, from question raised to decision binding; **rework volume attributable to misunderstanding**, which is what comprehension looks like when you measure it downstream rather than asking people whether they felt heard; and **authorship distribution** — whose documents get cited, whose proposals get adopted, by location. That last one is a proxy for whether influence actually moved or whether we merely distributed the typing.

Two qualitative practices I'd protect against every efficiency review. **Everyone with decision rights works one full day per quarter on another region's clock** — not visiting, not a courtesy call at 7am, the whole day. And **the misunderstanding corpus stays open and unsummarised**, read directly. Themes launder tone out of an incident, and tone is where the finding is.

The lagging indicator that tells the truth eventually: voluntary attrition, by site. The person who has taken the 11pm call for eighteen months does not complain. They leave.

---

## Sequencing, and the part I'd rather not announce

No programme name. No charter signed at an all-hands. Announcing a communication initiative invites everyone to perform good communication for six weeks, which contaminates the only data worth having, and hands anyone with a grudge a very convenient thing to be cynical about.

Weeks 0–4: the wait-state log, the incident corpus, the decision map. On two teams, quietly, with two comparable teams left alone.

Weeks 4–12: rotate or kill the standing meetings, written-decision default, escalation rungs deleted, and one workstream re-cut so that its boundaries fall where the clock already falls. Unannounced. Observed against the untouched teams.

Then travel, once there's a reason for people to want to meet each other. Then, and only then, tools — chosen against a workflow that by then actually exists, rather than a workflow the tool will invent for us.

The awkward possibility I'd want on the table from the beginning: **there may be no communication problem here at all.** There may simply be a headquarters — a place where the real conversation happens, surrounded by locations that receive its output and are asked to feel like peers. Every symptom in the brief is consistent with that, and none of it is fixable by anything a collaboration budget can buy.

And a second one, less comfortable still. Some of this work should probably never have been distributed. Splitting a tightly coupled problem across nine timezones to reach cheaper or scarcer talent is a trade in which the delay was *the price*, agreed in advance by someone who is no longer in the conversation. Complaining about the delay afterwards is complaining about having paid.

Worth establishing early which of those we're allowed to say out loud.
